title: Ectopic Pregnancy
clinical_background: Ectopic pregnancy involves implantation outside the uterine cavity and affects approximately 1% to 2% of pregnancies in the United States. It accounts for 2.7% of pregnancy-related deaths, and approximately 97% of cases occur in the fallopian tube. Tubal abnormalities, prior ectopic pregnancy, smoking, and certain contraceptive circumstances are among the risk factors discussed. Patients commonly present with lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding, while dizziness, fainting, shoulder pain, or severe pelvic pain may indicate rupture. Similar symptoms occur in other conditions, making prompt diagnosis important. Management depends on clinical stability, implantation site, β-hCG levels, and ultrasound findings, with attention to fertility preservation and psychological support.
objectives: Distinguish ectopic pregnancy from conditions with similar clinical presentations.
Accurately interpret diagnostic investigations used to evaluate ectopic pregnancy.
Select an appropriate management approach for each type of ectopic pregnancy.
Use interprofessional strategies to improve care coordination and outcomes for patients with ectopic pregnancy.
main_conclusion: Early recognition and treatment of ectopic pregnancy are essential to reduce the risk of rupture and severe hemorrhage. Management should reflect hemodynamic stability, implantation site, diagnostic findings, and the patient’s fertility goals, with urgent surgery when rupture is suspected.
narrative_summary:
This educational review examines the presentation, diagnosis, and management of ectopic pregnancy rather than reporting a new clinical study. Ectopic pregnancy affects approximately 1% to 2% of pregnancies in the United States and accounts for 2.7% of pregnancy-related deaths. Approximately 97% occur in the fallopian tube. Lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding are common, while dizziness, fainting, shoulder pain, or severe pelvic pain may indicate rupture.

Evaluation combines serum β-hCG measurements with ultrasound, particularly TVUS. A β-hCG level >2000 mIU/mL without a visible intrauterine pregnancy is highly suggestive of ectopic pregnancy; the review also notes a suggested discriminatory cutoff of up to 3500 mIU/mL to avoid misdiagnosing a viable pregnancy. When pregnancy location remains uncertain, serial β-hCG measurements and repeat imaging may be needed.

Hemodynamic instability or suspected rupture requires urgent surgical intervention. For selected asymptomatic patients with low, declining β-hCG, expectant management may be considered; 88% of ectopic pregnancies with an initial β-hCG level of <200 mIU/mL resolved spontaneously. In appropriate candidates, methotrexate is a medical option, with reported success of approximately 70% to 95%; β-hCG monitoring continues until the level is undetectable. Surgical options include salpingostomy and salpingectomy. For cesarean scar ectopic pregnancy, expectant management is not recommended except in select cases of confirmed fetal demise, and systemic methotrexate alone is not recommended.
interpretation: Early identification and treatment of ectopic pregnancy can substantially reduce severe complications, whereas delayed diagnosis may allow rupture, life-threatening hemorrhage, and loss of reproductive capacity. Management depends on hemodynamic stability, implantation site, β-hCG findings, ultrasound findings, and the patient’s fertility preferences. Selected stable patients may be managed expectantly or with methotrexate; suspected rupture requires urgent surgery.
clinical_implications: An intrauterine pregnancy does not rule out a simultaneous ectopic pregnancy.
A declining serum β-hCG level favors early pregnancy loss but does not, by itself, exclude an ectopic pregnancy.
Earlier diagnosis can broaden the scope for conservative treatment and fertility preservation.
Medical management with methotrexate succeeds in approximately 70% to 95% of patients, but success becomes less likely as the initial β-hCG level rises.

The single-dose methotrexate protocol has the fewest adverse effects; the 2-dose protocol has a lower treatment failure rate, particularly when initial β-hCG is higher. The multidose protocol entails more complex administration and follow-up and a greater risk of adverse effects.

Surgery has a higher success rate than methotrexate. Salpingostomy and salpingectomy have similar reported outcomes for subsequent intrauterine pregnancy and recurrent ectopic pregnancy; reproductive outcomes are also comparable between these procedures when the opposite fallopian tube is intact.
Interstitial ectopic pregnancy has limited capacity to expand and may lead to hemoperitoneum and life-threatening bleeding. A cesarean scar pregnancy can cause uterine rupture and severe hemorrhage.

A previous ectopic pregnancy increases recurrence risk, particularly when other underlying risk factors are present. Emotional distress and concerns about future fertility may persist after treatment.
practice_implications: Consider ectopic pregnancy in a sexually active woman of childbearing age who presents with abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding. Evaluate symptoms that may indicate rupture, including severe pelvic pain, dizziness, fainting, and shoulder pain, and assess hemodynamic stability promptly.

Use serum β-hCG measurements together with ultrasound for diagnosis. TVUS is the preferred imaging approach for early detection, with serial β-hCG measurements and repeat imaging when the pregnancy location remains uncertain.
For a stable patient whose β-hCG is falling but whose possible ectopic pregnancy has not been excluded, continue serial β-hCG monitoring until the level is undetectable.

Interpret a discriminatory β-hCG threshold cautiously: the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists suggests a cutoff of up to 3500 mIU/mL to reduce the risk of incorrectly diagnosing and ending a viable pregnancy.
For a pregnancy of unknown location (PUL), use serial β-hCG assessment and, in some cases, manual vacuum aspiration to help distinguish a failing intrauterine pregnancy from an ectopic pregnancy.
Transfer any patient with signs of ectopic pregnancy rupture urgently for surgical intervention.

Consider expectant management only in selected asymptomatic patients with low, declining β-hCG who accept the risks of tubal rupture and hemorrhage. Begin medical or surgical treatment if pain develops, β-hCG persists or rises, or signs of rupture appear.
Tailor the choice of medical or surgical treatment to clinical and ultrasound findings, serum β-hCG, and the patient’s reproductive goals and preferences.

Before giving methotrexate, assess contraindications and obtain a complete blood count and metabolic panel. Absolute contraindications listed include hemodynamic instability, anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, immunodeficiency, rupture, renal or hepatic dysfunction, unreliable follow-up, active pulmonary or peptic ulcer disease, and breastfeeding. Relative contraindications listed include fetal cardiac activity, serum β-hCG levels > 5000 mIU/mL or adenxal mass > 4 cm in diameter, and refusal of blood transfusion.

A 2-dose methotrexate regimen may be preferred, especially when treatment failure risk is high because of elevated β-hCG or a large adnexal mass. Some experts suggest considering a multidose regimen for more advanced gestation or an extratubal implantation site.

After methotrexate, measure serum β-hCG on days 4 and 7. A decline of at least 15% between those days indicates effective treatment; if it does not occur, additional methotrexate or surgery may be necessary. Continue weekly measurements until β-hCG is undetectable, which can take up to 8 weeks.

Counsel patients receiving methotrexate that rupture remains possible until β-hCG becomes undetectable and that worsening symptoms warrant emergency care. Advise avoidance of folic acid supplements, NSAIDs, alcohol, narcotics, vigorous exercise, and intercourse; discuss sun exposure and contraception for at least 1 ovulatory cycle after treatment, noting that some experts advise waiting 3 months.

Base the decision to preserve or remove the affected fallopian tube on intraoperative findings and fertility goals. Salpingectomy is preferred when tubal damage is substantial, rupture has occurred, or the patient previously underwent tubal ligation.

Do not recommend expectant management for cesarean scar ectopic pregnancy because of rupture and hemorrhage risk, except in selected cases with confirmed fetal demise. Do not recommend curettage alone because of hemorrhage and incomplete trophoblastic removal risks, or systemic methotrexate alone because of higher failure and complication rates.

For cesarean scar ectopic pregnancy, consider the described surgical approaches or local or intragestational methotrexate, often combined with systemic methotrexate, according to the clinical situation. Continue posttreatment surveillance because β-hCG and mass size may take weeks to resolve.

Educate patients about ectopic pregnancy symptoms, timely pregnancy testing, early prenatal assessment, and the need for immediate care for severe abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, dizziness, or fainting. Counsel on smoking cessation and prevention of sexually transmitted infections.

Closely monitor early pregnancy with serial β-hCG measurements and TVUS in patients undergoing fertility treatment or with known tubal abnormalities. Provide psychological support and address fertility concerns and recurrence during follow-up.
Coordinate diagnosis, treatment decisions, medication safety, patient education, and follow-up across the interprofessional healthcare team.
open_questions: A standardized treatment approach for cervical ectopic pregnancy has not been established.
future_directions: Further investigation is needed into the sensitivity and specificity of MRI for the diagnostic circumstances described.

secondary_results: The review describes TVUS as the most sensitive and accurate imaging approach for early ectopic pregnancy detection; visualization of an extrauterine yolk sac or embryo provides definitive confirmation. It provides no comparative accuracy estimates.
For pregnancy of unknown location, serial β-hCG assessment, repeat ultrasonography, and sometimes manual vacuum aspiration may help distinguish a failing IUP from ectopic pregnancy.

In early pregnancy, the double decidual sign is typically visible during the fifth week on abdominal ultrasonography; identification of the yolk sac around that time requires transvaginal imaging, and an embryonic pole can be visible transvaginally at approximately 6 weeks.

Histologic identification of villus-like structures, trophoblasts, or an embryo at an ectopic site is described as diagnostic. Spiegelberg's criteria comprise 4 findings used to distinguish ovarian ectopic pregnancy.

The review characterizes methotrexate as a folate antagonist that disrupts rapidly dividing cells and states that medically treated patients have higher fertility rates than surgically treated patients, without giving comparative estimates.

Compared with the single-dose methotrexate protocol, the 2-dose protocol is described as more effective and less likely to fail, particularly when initial β-hCG is higher; the single-dose protocol has fewer adverse effects. No comparative effect estimates are given.
Surgery is described as having a higher treatment success rate than methotrexate, without a numerical comparison.

Salpingostomy and salpingectomy are described as yielding similar subsequent IUP and ectopic recurrence outcomes. Reproductive outcomes are also described as comparable between these procedures when the contralateral tube is intact; no rates are provided.

For cesarean scar ectopic pregnancy, the review advises against expectant management because of rupture and hemorrhage risk, apart from selected cases with confirmed fetal demise. It also advises against curettage alone because of hemorrhage and incomplete trophoblastic removal, and against systemic methotrexate alone because of higher failure and complication rates.
The review reports low complication rates with transvaginal or laparoscopic resection of cesarean scar ectopic pregnancy but gives no numerical rates.
After treatment of cesarean scar ectopic pregnancy, β-hCG levels and mass size may take weeks to resolve; no quantified resolution rate is reported.

The review states that identifying and treating ectopic pregnancy before rupture significantly reduces severe complications, whereas delayed diagnosis can lead to life-threatening hemorrhage and hemodynamic instability.

document_sections.heading: Continuing Education Activity
document_sections.content: Ectopic pregnancy is implantation of a fertilized egg outside the uterus, usually in a fallopian tube. It affects approximately 1% to 2% of pregnancies in the United States, and rupture is estimated to cause 2.7% of pregnancy-related deaths. Risk factors include pelvic inflammatory disease, smoking, previous ectopic pregnancy, tubal surgery, and infertility. Lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy warrant particular concern when an intrauterine pregnancy has not been confirmed. The educational activity addresses diagnostic difficulties, differential diagnoses, fertility preservation, psychological support, and management options. It aims to improve prompt recognition, appropriate evaluation, and coordinated interprofessional care.

document_sections.heading: Objectives:
document_sections.content: The learning objectives are to distinguish ectopic pregnancy from conditions with similar presentations, interpret diagnostic findings, select management appropriate to the type of ectopic pregnancy, and use interprofessional teamwork to improve care coordination and outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Ectopic pregnancy involves implantation outside the uterine cavity, affects approximately 1% to 2% of pregnancies in the United States, can be life-threatening, and accounts for 2.7% of pregnancy-related deaths. Approximately 97% occur in a fallopian tube, often in association with tubal abnormalities. Potential causes of these abnormalities include gonorrhea, chlamydia, tubal surgery including sterilization, previous ectopic pregnancy, and exposure to diethylstilbestrol in utero. Conception during use of intrauterine devices (IUDs) or progesterone-only contraceptives is another risk factor. Less common implantation sites include the cervix, ovary, abdomen, uterine cornua, and cesarean scars. These extratubal pregnancies are less consistently linked to usual risk factors or tubal disease and can be especially difficult to diagnose and manage. Early detection, whatever the site, supports conservative treatment and better outcomes. Typical symptoms are lower abdominal pain, often unilateral, and vaginal bleeding; dizziness, fainting, shoulder pain, or severe pelvic pain can suggest rupture. Early normal intrauterine pregnancy, miscarriage, ovarian cyst rupture, and appendicitis can resemble ectopic pregnancy, so timely assessment is important. Management seeks to preserve fertility, improve diagnostic accuracy, and offer psychological support. Clinical stability, implantation site, beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG), and ultrasound findings guide choices from observation to surgery. Methotrexate may work in selected, early-diagnosed cases meeting treatment criteria, but success is less likely with larger masses, higher β-hCG, or a visible embryo. Advanced or ruptured pregnancy generally requires urgent surgery.

document_sections.heading: Etiology
document_sections.content: An ectopic pregnancy is an embryo implanted outside the uterine cavity. The fallopian tube is the most frequent site, although implantation can occur in a cesarean scar, endocervical canal, ovary, or peritoneal cavity. Within the tube, the ampulla accounts for 70%; other possible sites include the cornua, fimbriae, and proximal isthmic segment. A heterotopic pregnancy combines an ectopic pregnancy with a normally developing pregnancy in the endometrial cavity. Tubal injury can impair transport and retain an oocyte or embryo; tubal ligation and other surgical changes can likewise alter tubal function. Extranubal implantation need not involve tubal dysfunction or customary risk factors. Recurrence risk is 10% after 1 previous ectopic pregnancy and >25% after 2 or more. Additional associated factors are tubal damage from gonorrhea, chlamydia, pelvic or tubal surgery, or endometriosis; pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) or complications of ascending infection; and infertility or assisted reproductive technology. With assisted reproduction, risk is higher with more embryo transfers, fresh rather than frozen transfers, and cleavage-stage (Day 3) transfers. IUD users have a lower overall risk of pregnancy, but 53% of pregnancies arising with an IUD are ectopic. Smoking is associated with increased risk through effects on tubal function. Women older than 35, those with congenital reproductive tract anomalies, and those with previous cesarean delivery—particularly after breech presentation—may have increased risk. Progesterone-only contraception carries a slightly higher risk than other contraceptive methods. Conversely, oral contraceptives, previous pregnancy termination, failure of emergency contraception, and cesarean delivery are described as not associated with increased risk.

document_sections.heading: Epidemiology
document_sections.content: Ectopic pregnancies account for approximately 1% to 2% of pregnancies in the United States and 2% to 5% among patients using assisted reproductive technology. Emergency departments report an incidence of 6% to 16%. Cases treated outside hospitals may make the true prevalence higher than estimated. Mortality from rupture has declined over recent decades, but ruptured pregnancies still contribute to pregnancy-related deaths. Tubal implantation is most common; its rupture rate is around 15% in Western countries and may have risen during the COVID-19 pandemic. Cervical implantation has an incidence of <1%; dilation and curettage preceded it in 70% of these patients. Ovarian implantation occurs in <3% of cases and abdominal implantation in 0.9% to 1.4%. Abdominal pregnancy has higher mortality than other ectopic types, at 10%; delayed diagnosis occurs more often, and the risk of organ perforation and massive hemorrhage is up to 7 times higher. Interstitial implantation accounts for up to 4% of ectopic sites. Omental, retroperitoneal, splenic, and hepatic implantation have also been reported. Cesarean deliveries currently constitute 21% of births worldwide; their increasing frequency may raise the incidence of cesarean-scar pregnancy, which is approximately <1%. Assisted reproductive technology has increased heterotopic pregnancy incidence, and in vitro fertilization increases the likelihood of ectopic implantation. Estimated heterotopic pregnancy risk reaches as high as 1:100 among women seeking in vitro fertilization. Ectopic pregnancy occurs in 2.1% to 8.6% of in vitro fertilization conceptions versus around 2% of natural pregnancies.

document_sections.heading: Pathophysiology
document_sections.content: Tubal smooth-muscle contractions and ciliary movement help move the oocyte or embryo toward the uterine cavity. Usually inflammation-related tubal injury can disrupt that transport and retain the oocyte or embryo in the tube. Toxic, infectious, immunologic, and hormonal factors can produce local inflammation. Following tubal damage, increased proinflammatory cytokine activity encourages implantation, invasion, and angiogenesis in the tube. Chlamydia trachomatis prompts tubal epithelial cells to produce interleukin 1, described as an important signal for endometrial embryo implantation; interleukin 1 also recruits neutrophils, potentially adding to tubal damage. Smoking and infection reduce ciliary beat frequency, which also varies with hormonal changes over the menstrual cycle.

document_sections.heading: Histopathology
document_sections.content: The tubal ampulla is the most frequent attachment site. Reportedly, 95% of ectopic pregnancies arise in the ampullary, infundibular, or isthmic portions of the tubes. Histologic identification of villus-like structures, trophoblasts, or an embryo in a tube or another ectopic site establishes the diagnosis. Spiegelberg's criteria are often used to distinguish ovarian implantation from other sites and require 4 findings: a fallopian tube intact and separate from the affected ovary; a gestational sac occupying the ovary's position; attachment of that ovary to the uterus through the ovarian ligament; and ovarian tissue both attached to and present within the gestational-sac wall. In cesarean-scar pregnancy, residual scar defects permit blastocyst migration into the myometrium. Histology shows villous invasion of myometrial or scar tissue with little decidua. Implantation depth defines type 1, nearer the uterine wall, and type 2, nearer the urinary bladder.

document_sections.heading: Clinical History
document_sections.content: Adnexal ectopic pregnancy often begins with variable, colicky abdominal or pelvic pain, commonly on one side, but that pattern is not universal. Tubal distension can progress to more diffuse pain if rupture and hemoperitoneum develop. Other possible symptoms are dizziness, fainting, nausea, vomiting, shoulder pain, urinary complaints, and rectal pressure; women of childbearing age with these symptoms should be evaluated. Cesarean-scar pregnancy can be asymptomatic when found on routine obstetric ultrasound or present with uterine rupture. History should establish the last menstrual period, menstrual regularity, sexual activity, and ectopic pregnancy risk factors. A missed period, abnormal uterine bleeding, or sexual activity can indicate possible pregnancy and warrant pregnancy testing.

document_sections.heading: Physical Examination
document_sections.content: A careful examination helps direct diagnostic testing. Vital signs should be assessed for tachycardia and hypotension to determine hemodynamic stability. Abdominal and suprapubic examination should identify where tenderness occurs and what worsens it. Voluntary or involuntary guarding on palpation raises concern for free fluid associated with ectopic rupture or for peritonitis. A palpable gravid uterus can suggest intrauterine pregnancy but does not rule out ectopic or heterotopic pregnancy. Pelvic examination should assess vaginal bleeding, cervical abnormalities, dilation of the cervical os, visible products of conception, and infection. Bimanual examination can detect adnexal masses or tenderness on either side.

document_sections.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation of Ectopic Pregnancy
document_sections.content: Evaluation principally combines serum beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) measurement with transvaginal ultrasonography (TVUS) and transabdominal ultrasonography (TAUS). TVUS is described as the most sensitive and accurate method for early detection, particularly with 3-dimensional imaging and color Doppler ultrasound. A β-hCG level >2000 mIU/mL without a visible intrauterine pregnancy (IUP) strongly suggests ectopic pregnancy. In a viable IUP starting at β-hCG <1500 mIU/mL, there is a 99% likelihood of a minimum 49% increase over 48 hours. A slower increase or a decline of at least 21% over 48 hours points more toward miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy; falling serum β-hCG more strongly suggests spontaneous early pregnancy loss. The discriminatory β-hCG threshold above which TVUS should show an IUP depends on equipment, operator expertise, and gestational number. Although historically between 1000 and 2000 mIU/mL, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists has suggested a cutoff of up to 3500 mIU/mL to reduce misdiagnosis and avoid unnecessary termination of a viable pregnancy. Stable patients whose β-hCG is falling but whose possible ectopic pregnancy remains unexcluded should have serial measurements until β-hCG becomes undetectable. TVUS is the diagnostic gold standard; visualization of a yolk sac or embryo outside the uterus confirms ectopic pregnancy. Because many cases do not develop far enough for this finding, serial β-hCG tests, repeat ultrasound, or uterine aspiration may be needed. When neither IUP nor ectopic pregnancy is identified, the designation is pregnancy of unknown location (PUL); serial β-hCG and sometimes manual vacuum aspiration can distinguish a failing IUP from ectopic pregnancy. Serial transvaginal imaging, serum hCG measurements, or both are required for confirmation. The earliest ultrasonographic IUP finding is a small sac eccentrically placed in the decidua; surrounding tissue rings produce the “double decidual” sign. This sign is typically apparent in the fifth week of pregnancy on abdominal ultrasound. The yolk sac appears around the same time but is accurately identified with transvaginal imaging. A transvaginal scan can show an embryonic pole at approximately 6 weeks of pregnancy. Fibroids or a high body mass index can reduce ultrasound accuracy for an early IUP. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may help in extreme circumstances, such as large obstructing fibroids, but its sensitivity and specificity need further study, and risks of gadolinium contrast exposure require careful consideration.

document_sections.heading: Diagnostic Findings of Non-Fallopian Tube Pregnancies
document_sections.content: TVUS now permits earlier recognition of cervical pregnancy, which was previously often diagnosed in the second trimester or during spontaneous abortion. No standardized treatment exists, although conservative options that preserve fertility are available. TVUS alone has difficulty distinguishing ovarian ectopic pregnancy from a hemorrhagic cyst, so histopathologic confirmation using Spiegelberg’s criteria is often needed. Rare abdominal implantations can involve the retroperitoneum, liver, spleen, appendix, or lung and are frequently discovered only at surgery. Fetal malpresentation, oligohydramnios, and increased maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein can provide diagnostic clues. For cesarean-scar pregnancy, TVUS, commonly supplemented by color Doppler, is preferred. Suggestive findings are an anterior low-lying gestational sac in the hysterotomy scar, little or no myometrium between sac and bladder, and prominent vascularity at the scar. Magnetic resonance imaging may also aid diagnosis. Early recognition is important to prevent uterine rupture and severe hemorrhage. Findings suggestive of interstitial implantation on TVUS are the interstitial line sign, an eccentric gestational sac, and a surrounding myometrial mantle <5 mm thick. Three-dimensional sonography improves detection, and MRI can assist when findings remain inconclusive. Distinguishing interstitial from cornual pregnancy matters: interstitial ectopic pregnancy has less room to expand and is linked to hemoperitoneum and life-threatening bleeding, whereas some cornual pregnancies can continue without spontaneous abortion but carry risks of persistent vaginal bleeding, retained placenta at delivery, and uterine rupture.

document_sections.heading: Management of Ectopic Pregnancy
document_sections.content: Treatment addresses the ectopic gestation while preserving reproductive potential as far as possible when the patient wishes. Future fertility preferences should therefore inform the choice of intervention. Hemodynamic status determines the initial approach, and signs of rupture require urgent transfer for surgery. When diagnosis is early, the patient is stable, and the affected tube remains intact, options include intramuscular methotrexate, salpingostomy to remove the pregnancy while retaining the tube, or salpingectomy to remove part or all of that tube. Clinical findings, ultrasound, serum βhCG, and patient preference inform selection between medication and surgery. With initial β-hCG <200 mIU/mL, 88% of ectopic pregnancies resolved spontaneously under expectant management. Although rarely used, observation may be considered for selected asymptomatic patients with low and declining β-hCG who accept the risks of tubal rupture and hemorrhage. Pain, persistent or rising β-hCG, or signs of tubal rupture instead warrant medical or surgical treatment.

document_sections.heading: Medical management
document_sections.content: Surgery definitively removes an ectopic pregnancy, but the article reports higher fertility rates after medical treatment with methotrexate; it may therefore be preferred by suitable patients wishing to retain fertility options. Methotrexate is a folate antagonist that interferes with rapidly dividing cells and is the only medication described for medical management. Treatment succeeds in approximately 70% to 95% of patients, with lower efficacy as initial β-hCG rises. Absolute contraindications are hemodynamic instability; anemia, leukopenia, or thrombocytopenia; immunodeficiency; rupture; renal or hepatic dysfunction; unreliable follow-up; active pulmonary or peptic ulcer disease; and breastfeeding. Relative contraindications are fetal cardiac activity, serum β-hCG > 5000 mIU/mL or an adnexal mass > 4 cm in diameter, and refusal of blood transfusion. Patients should be checked for contraindications before treatment, including with a complete blood count and metabolic panel. Available protocols are single-dose, 2-dose, and multidose. Single-dose treatment has the fewest adverse effects; the 2-dose protocol is more effective and fails less often, especially with higher starting β-hCG. A 2-dose regimen may generally be favored, particularly when high β-hCG or a large adnexal mass raises failure risk. Multidose treatment is less favored because administration and follow-up are more complex and adverse effects more frequent, although some experts suggest considering it for advanced gestation or extratubal sites such as cervical or ovarian pregnancy. Serum β-hCG is checked on days 4 and 7 after methotrexate. A decrease of at least 15% between days 4 and 7 indicates response; otherwise, further methotrexate or surgery may be necessary. Testing continues weekly until β-hCG is undetectable, potentially taking up to 8 weeks. Patients should be informed that rupture remains possible until then and should seek emergency care for worsening symptoms. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, vaginal spotting, and temporary hair loss. Patients should avoid folic acid supplements, NSAIDs, alcohol, narcotics, vigorous exercise, and intercourse because of treatment interactions or rupture risk. Sun exposure can cause methotrexate dermatitis. Contraception is advised for at least 1 ovulatory cycle after treatment; some experts advise waiting 3 months. Studies cited by the article suggest methotrexate does not impair future fertility.

document_sections.heading: Surgical management
document_sections.content: Surgery has a higher success rate than methotrexate. Reasons to consider it include β-hCG typically >5,000 mIU/mL, an embryo with cardiac activity on ultrasound, and circumstances limiting access to follow-up. Laparoscopy is commonly performed when methotrexate is contraindicated or not preferred. Salpingectomy removes some or all of the affected tube; salpingostomy, also termed salpingotomy, removes the ectopic pregnancy through a tubal incision while retaining the tube. The procedures produce similar subsequent intrauterine pregnancy and ectopic recurrence outcomes. Intraoperative findings and fertility goals guide whether the tube is retained. Significant tubal damage, rupture, or earlier tubal ligation favor salpingectomy. With an intact opposite tube, reproductive outcomes are comparable between the procedures. For interstitial pregnancy, hysterectomy may be required in severe hemorrhage or when fertility preservation is not desired.

document_sections.heading: Cervical and Cesarean Scar Ectopic Pregnancy
document_sections.content: Cervical and cesarean-scar pregnancies need specialized management. Expectant management of cesarean-scar pregnancy is not recommended because of uterine rupture and hemorrhage risk, apart from selected cases with confirmed fetal demise. Transvaginal or laparoscopic resection has shown low complication rates. Curettage alone is not recommended because bleeding and incomplete trophoblastic removal are risks. Hysterectomy may be considered if fertility preservation is not a priority. Medical treatment of cesarean-scar pregnancy usually uses local or intragestational methotrexate, frequently combined with systemic methotrexate. Systemic methotrexate alone is not recommended because failure and complications are more frequent. Ultrasound-guided aspiration can supplement medication. Follow-up is essential because β-hCG and mass size may require weeks to resolve.

document_sections.heading: Differential Diagnosis
document_sections.content: Conditions to consider include ovarian torsion, tubo-ovarian abscess, appendicitis, hemorrhagic corpus luteum, ruptured ovarian cyst, threatened miscarriage, incomplete miscarriage, pelvic inflammatory disease, and ureteral calculi.

document_sections.heading: Prognosis
document_sections.content: Outcome depends on early diagnosis and timely treatment. Medical treatment with methotrexate or surgery before rupture significantly reduces the risk of severe complications. Delayed diagnosis can allow tubal rupture, life-threatening hemorrhage, and hemodynamic instability, requiring emergency surgery that may include salpingectomy and affect later fertility. Previous ectopic pregnancy increases recurrence risk, particularly with preceding tubal surgery, pelvic inflammatory disease, or assisted reproductive technology. Most patients recover well with appropriate treatment, but longer-term follow-up matters for fertility concerns and possible recurrence.

document_sections.heading: Complications
document_sections.content: Potential complications are tubal rupture, severe hemorrhage, need for blood transfusion, hemodynamic shock progressing to multiorgan failure, impaired fertility, recurrent ectopic pregnancy, adhesions, and emotional or psychological distress.

document_sections.heading: Deterrence and Patient Education
document_sections.content: Education can help lower risk and improve early recognition, particularly for patients with pelvic inflammatory disease, previous ectopic pregnancy, tubal surgery, or infertility treatment. Patients should learn the symptoms and the importance of early prenatal care; timely pregnancy testing and early ultrasound may identify ectopic pregnancy before complications. Severe abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, dizziness, or fainting warrant immediate medical assessment because they can signal rupture. Counseling should address smoking cessation and prevention of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) through safer sexual practices to reduce tubal injury and future ectopic pregnancy. Patients receiving fertility treatment or known to have tubal abnormalities should be closely monitored early in pregnancy with serial β-hCG and transvaginal ultrasound. Emotional support and access to counseling can help with psychological effects and fertility concerns. Patients receiving methotrexate may need to discuss foods, supplements, and medicines to avoid with their obstetrician because adverse interactions can reduce efficacy; combinations with other medications may also increase immunosuppression or cause other adverse effects. After surgery, patients should follow their surgeon's instructions to reduce infection and other postoperative complications.

document_sections.heading: Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
document_sections.content: Accurate diagnosis, timely treatment, and favorable outcomes depend on coordinated care among nurses, emergency physicians, obstetricians, advanced practitioners, pharmacists, and other specialists. In the emergency department, nurses help recognize concerning symptoms and arrange prompt clinician assessment. Clinicians should consider ectopic pregnancy in sexually active women of childbearing age who have abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding. Evidence-based tools, standardized protocols, and clinical decision-making models can improve diagnostic accuracy and efficiency while limiting unnecessary tests and delays. Emergency physicians and obstetricians should collaborate on confirmation, treatment selection, and discussion of options with the patient; communication with radiologists and pharmacists is also important. Pharmacists support safe methotrexate administration and education about adverse effects and monitoring. Nurses provide education, emotional support, and posttreatment follow-up, reinforce adherence, and help identify complications. Clear interprofessional communication and teamwork support patient-centered care and safety.

document_sections.heading: Figures
document_sections.content: The figure descriptions include a positive FAST examination in the RUQ of a patient with suspected ectopic pregnancy, with free fluid at the caudal liver tip, right paracolic gutter, and hepatorenal (Morrison's) pouch. Other images depict an ectopic pregnancy on ultrasound, implantation in the endocervical canal, and a left tubal ectopic pregnancy with substantial adhesions to the pelvic sidewall.
